Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
With the upcoming Camarilla set doubtless featuring
lots of reprints, I thought this would be an
appropriate time to bring up the issue of rarity
selection.

It seems to me that it's good for the game - on a
playability level - for everyone who likes competitive
play to be able to get all the cards they want to make
the decks they want to make. Given that, I'd expect
that things like Freak Drive, Immortal Grapple, Awe,
Temptation, probably even things like Disarm, Temptation
of Greater Power, Hostile Takeover, should be uncommon
rather than rare. (The move of Grapple to uncommon in
Sabbat is one of the best decisions I think WotC ever
made.) (Things like Coagulated Entity, Gift of Bellona,
Hag's Wrinkles, Rewind Time, too, though they're
probably much too recent to get reprinted already. ;-)

Is this a point of view that's generally taken for
granted, or more questionable than I think? I can
see that, taken to its logical conclusion, my argument
would suggest that rarity should be entirely flat (ie
everything the same rarity) and apparently that's
undesirable in CCGs for profitability reasons, but
I do think that some flattening of rarity would be
good for the game, and possibly even good for the
game-publisher in that people would be less likely to
become frustrated by the difficulty of collecting
a set designed in this fashion.

Comments? Agreement? Dissent?

Josh

While this is true, it certainly isn't practically possible - there's a
number of cards that are particularly powerful but in only one kind of
deck, which makes them impossible to get while everyone wants to try
that deck (e.g. Armor of Terra Gargoyles), but which are completely and
utterly useless to someone who decides not to bother with that kind of
deck.
To allow everyone to build that particular deck, these cards would have
to be uncommon, but that might not necessarily be a good idea.

> Given that, I'd expect
> that things like Freak Drive, Immortal Grapple, Awe,
> Temptation, probably even things like Disarm, Temptation
> of Greater Power, Hostile Takeover, should be uncommon
> rather than rare.

Freak Drive and Awe are very good examples of cards that indeed should
be uncommon in a game that bases rarity on card utility, being very
useful in a number of different decks built around many vampires of
various clans. [Any deck benefits from being able to untap a vampire, so
Freak Drive might as well be common (most common cards require a
discipline).]
Temptation of Greater power is not: there's exactly seven vampires that
can use a Justicar only card - so the card is only useful in a deck
built around it.

> (The move of Grapple to uncommon in
> Sabbat is one of the best decisions I think WotC ever
> made.)

That is so true... and even so, IG isn't exactly easy to come by.

> (Things like Coagulated Entity, Gift of Bellona,
> Hag's Wrinkles, Rewind Time, too, though they're
> probably much too recent to get reprinted already. ;-)

Some of these are extremely specific cards so their being rare may well
be justified... there's currently 3 vampires that can use Rewind Time
(and that probably won't change anytime soon), so it's perfectly
legitimate this card is rare.

>
> Is this a point of view that's generally taken for
> granted, or more questionable than I think?

> I can
> see that, taken to its logical conclusion, my argument

WW seemed to think a non-flat rare-heavy distribution was the way to go
with Bloodlines, and while sone of the R1s are indeed mostly useless,
there's quite a few that should not have been ultra-rare (Armor of Terra
again comes to mind - just because it's only useful in one deck, it
shouldn't be so rare that said deck is all but impossible to assemble. I
managed to trade for it because one player gave up on trying to get 5-6
of them, and while I'm happy I finally got one, I very seriously doubt
that's a sign of BL rarity distribution actually having helped the
game).

> but
> I do think that some flattening of rarity would be
> good for the game, and possibly even good for the
> game-publisher in that people would be less likely to
> become frustrated by the difficulty of collecting
> a set designed in this fashion.

I totally agree. I'd very much like to see R1s disappear from VTES, with
a shift toward more C1s - there were so many C2s in FN and BL that had
no place being C2s, anyway.

Anyone that has ever used more Masquers than they got from their
Giovanni starters alone? So maybe the Path of Bone could have been C1
along with Masquer (hey, the AH paths were common, the SW paths
uncommon, so why exactly is this one so much less useful it has to be
rare?), and Augustus R2 instead of ultra-rare. [Repeat with 7 other
cards to get a flat 50xR2 sheet and a handful of extra C1s.]

Does anyone understand why Sense Vitality is C2 while Engling Fury is
R1? The out-feriors are identical, the in-disciplines both are equally
worth 2 blood, but the condition for playing in-discipline Sense
Vitality [one ready vampire and a vampire in torpor somewhere] is more
restrictive than the one for Engling Fury [one ready vampire]. Seems to
me they could be both the same rarity, like, say, C1. [Any R1 of choice
becomes R2 as a result. How about Armor of Terra?]
Of course, with the untap effect, Engling Fury is slightly more powerful
(when used on your own vampires) than Sense Vitality, but since WW
doesn't rarify power cards, that can't possibly be the explanation for
why one is R1 and one is C2.

> Comments? Agreement? Dissent?

It's probably become evident that I don't believe the "utility based
rarity" fairy-tale, and think the current scheme is a profit-based one
that is not exactly in the best interest of the game.

I'm not going to pre-order the Camarilla set, because I'm not interested
in buying another set with a distribution optimized for profit rather
than playability, and certainly won't buy any of it unless I hear good
things about it's rarity distribution.

As a hint, Freak Drive should be R2 or better - making it R1 would be
all the proof it takes that WW does rarify power cards (and would make
me not buy another pack of VTES, ever).

Thomas

Yes. *Card* rarity is a lousy way to enforce *use* rarity. For
use rarity, the card should be less valuable - e.g. an Embrace costs pool
as well as blood, etc. If such cards exist and are common, you just
have to plan for everybody having a pile. If they're rare, the suitcases
will tend to drive off the normal players and you *still* have to plan
for everybody having a bunch, because you're left with suitcases who do.

Ideally, rare cards would be useful in exotic decks but only there, and the
exotic decks should be no better than regular decks. That's a tough goal,
though.

I figured there must be some people who feel this way - and
I can understand it to some degree - but I have to admit
it doesn't convince me. To me it seems like a perverse
embracing of frustration. :-) Getting, say, 12 Freak
Drives is absurdly hard to do without buying vast quantities
(and I do mean vast - there were about 100 rares in Jyhad;
at 36 rares per booster box you'd need 3 boxes per set or
36 boxes for 12 of each rare) of cards. And there are
many, many possible decks that can use lots of Freak Drives.

Your argument (like mine) becomes silly if taken to its
logical extreme - if it's fun to have things be hard to
get, then it'd be more fun if *everything* was rare, right?
;-) (Of course, if everything is rare, then nothing is,
but that's not the point.)

My philosophy here boils down to "cards people want lots
of shouldn't be rare". It's sort of an extension of "the
good cards shouldn't all be rare". From my point of view,
probably the most appropriately-rare cards would be
uniques (not to say that *every* unique should be rare,
but generally you won't want to build a deck around 5+
copies of a unique card). After that, effects that are
extremely specialized can be rare - things like Hostile
Takeover and Temptation of Greater Power may qualify,
along with things like Kine Dominance, Entrancement, and
Far Mastery. As the game turned out, cards like Shattering
Blow, Fast Hands, and Canine Horde probably could've been
rare too.

The problem I suppose you run into is, you don't want the
rares to suck, either. You want them to be interesting,
so that people are excited about getting more rares when
they open packs. But they *really* shouldn't (IMO) be
cards that have really staple-type effects, like Awe,
Freak Drive, The Embrace (as Ian pointed out), probably
Flesh of Marble.

> I prefer the status quo. If it's not broke, then don't fix it! The game is

have
> players do *some* work before putting together a ToGP or a Betrayer deck.

But why should they have to do so much work collecting
before they can play? Sure, it's a CCG, and part of
being involved with it is collecting. But it seems to
me that making things excessively rare only limits the
variety of potential decks people can make, almost like
a de facto CL.

Josh

favor of, something has to be rare. For this game, clan specific cards are
always candidates, cards that have no close substitutes are always candidates,
and so forth.

Putting aside whether these cards have too much utility, in fact, putting aside

normally a weakness of that whatever, the card should be rarer. Behind You!

of stealth. Now, does this criterion make sense? Probably not, as you either
end up with a crap card that doesn't fit its whatever or the card is so good
that you want "lots" of copies of a rare card.

Erm, if I recall correctly (and it's games I never played much so I
could easily be wrong):

The basic design plan was to create expansions of 150 cards each. This
is roughly equivalent to Dark Sovereigns or Ancient Hearts for us.

However, a number of games effectively produce a new basic set each
year. So three 150 card expansions would give you 450 cards. (The
exact numbers may vary, but these are the rough ballparks.) So if we
design three mini-expansions a year, we can regard them as a 'full'
expansion for that year.

In V:TES equivalent, that might be like producing a set for the Ravnos
and Giovanni, a set for the Assamites and Setites and a set for the
Tzimisce and Lasombra of about 150 cards each.

Now, instead of releasing this in one 450 card bunch, we decide to
release it in smaller packets. And instead of just randomly doing it,
we keep each mini-expansion together. And then, instead of releasing
each mini-expansion in one bunch, we split it up further. So,
effectively, you get:

January 1st - Release 50 Ravnos and Giovanni cards (Dark Sovereigns 1)
February 1st - Release 50 Ravnos and Giovanni cards (DS 2)
March 1st - Release 50 Ravnos and Giovanni cards (DS 3, final batch)
April 1st - Release 50 Assamite and Setite cards (Ancient Hearts 1)
May 1st - Release 50 Assamite and Setite cards (AH 2)
June 1st - Release 50 Assamite and Setite cards (AH 3, final batch)
July 1st - Release 50 Lasombra and Tzimisce cards (Sabbat 1)
August 1st - Release 50 Lasombra and Tzimisce cards (S 2)
September 1st - Release 50 Lasombra and Tzimisce cards (S3, final batch)
October }
November } Release nothing, allowing a period of equilibrium
December }

This is kind of equivalent to Magic releasing things like Mirage one
month (with a lot of basic cards in it), then releasing Mirage expansion
1 a few months later, and Mirage expansion 2 a bit later still.

As the web-page notes, this skeletal idea was manipulated for each set
it was tried on.

Most people I saw tended to buy the 'half-boxes' then trade for anything
they were missing. Unlike V:TES, of course, in games with card limits
you *can* buy more cards but the spares you get end up being mostly
redundant, whereas in V:TES you *can* buy trucks of cards and get
utility from them, or you can just buy singles from traders - up to you.

One pseudo-nice thing with buying expansions that come out at once,
also, is that you can just have one splurge and then recover. I wonder
how many people could say they were going to spend $200 on their hobby
every now and then and get away with it compared to someone who was
going to spend $70 every month. (Adjust figures to taste.) It's odd in
that slow-release delivery should allow you to plan but in the end, I'm
not sure.

Then there's the fact that it does seem a lot like Big Brother is
watching you. If I buy Ancient Hearts, I buy Ancient Hearts. I get all
the cards Ancient Hearts offers in half a dozen boosters, random
assortment. Now, if you split up Ancient Hearts so that Return to
Innocence went in that month, Tomb of Rameses III went in the next month
and Alamut goes in next month, and then have Contracts in month 1, Taste
of Death in month 2 and Khabar: Honor in month 3, well, it all looks a
bit suspect.

making all the hosers hose weenie vamps to a lesser extent
would probably have other benefits, too.

There is a risk to this card, though - if it's good enough against
non-Gangrel it'll be everywhere and the Gangrel become unplayable.
Toreador's bane averts this by being disciplinary. It's harder to
balance clan-plus hosers than clan hosers. The value of clan
hoser is proportional to the play rate for the clan; it's existence
cannot make a clan completely unplayable. With a clan+ hoser
the value ranges only over (non-clan value) to (non-clan value) +
(clan value)*(clan play rate). With 20 clans, that tends to be
a narrow spread.

But let's look at it this way. Yes, TB is a Tor/!Tor hoser. It can
also be played against younger vampires or allies.

It requires Melpominee, a discipline that is on a total of five
minions, the average capacity of which is 4. I've only seen TB played
once - against a Toreador Antitribu. Usually, the player of the DoC
is using the youngest vamps on the table.

Of course, my entire playgroup has gravitated away from weenies for
the most part, so that does affect the playability of the card, but
it's a relevant point.

Now, if there's no limitation on when you can play it (as you would
have with a master card), the playability of the card goes up
tremendously. The example you cite is TOO powerful - it makes it
impossible for a Gangrel deck to oust, and because it's decisively
anti-weenie, many decks will use it for that effect alone. Who'd play
Gangrel with that card out?

High-utility clan hosers either need to be temporary transient effects
(like Toreador's Bane), or cards that can be removed (Troile's Revenge
is an example). If it permanently destroys the game for the person
playing that clan, and can be played to foil entire strategies as
well, then you're telling the players not to play that clan at all.

Not while it still has the Hi Pro Glo on it.

When a game first comes out, it does one of two things. It either
succeeds because gameplay/story are worth the learning curve and
initial investment (as Doomtown did), or it fails miserably (as 2/3 of
all CCGs do).

The rarity scheme had nothing to do with this - since it was still
new, all the cards were equally rare to the new players, and the
episodic releases actually helped it, since new cards kept on coming.
This helps generate interest in a brand new game.

> You'd say "stuff you" and walk, and that's exactly what happened to Rage, so >it's being dead from the restart proves exactly zilch with regard to rarities.

LBS faltered from the get-go. The game wasn't nearly engaging enough
from all accounts I've heard to warrant people investing in the second
and future sequences.

The software store I worked at got into CCGs as a sideline when Dune
first came out. We got a large supply of Dune - which never sold.
Not even impulse buyers took notice of it. We eventually cleared it
off and wrote it off as a loss when we needed more room for Magic
cards (which we couldn't keep in stock for more than two days - so it
wasn't that CCG players weren't seeing them). From talking to game
shop owners in my area, their Dune stock met much the same fate. I
believe it was an ill-advised license (Dune fans make up a larger
number of wargamers than CCG players, which are a younger audience on
average), as well as a poorly executed design.

L5R - L5R was probably the second most successful card game on the
market before Scorpion Clan Coup. When I got into it, it was more
popular than Magic or VTES in the stores I frequented, and I wasted a
whole summer in that shop, playing L5R among other games. Where
Rolling Thunder helped Doomtown, it doomed L5R.

L5R players already had a large stock of cards when Scorpion Clan Coup
came out. Now, in order to get the new cards, they'd have to buy
boosters of cards they already had - a problem I already had with
earlier L5R expansions was that certain cards appeared in every single
expansion. Now, those cards are going to appear in three times the
volume over the span of a single expansion. Wonderful.

Under the tiered rarity system you see in Magic, VTES, and other
games, when you open a pack, you're going to see a lot of cards you
have PLENTY of, a few cards you have "enough, or close to enough" of,
and a card that you MIGHT have one or two of (unless you're really
gung ho, or really unlucky).

Imagine my frustration when I opened my first three packs of Hidden
Emporer, and got no cards I didn't already own from previous
expansions.

It's the same problem I had with Sabbat War (90% of my SW rares come
from a list of 10 Sabbat Rares I had enough of before SW came out).
At least with SW, I'm happy that I'm getting new product at all, and
there's justification in that they were the first VTES cards to be
printed AT ALL in four years.

L5R didn't have that justification. They just crammed the same old
cards into every single set - and now, if you bought all nine episodes
of a story, you got those same old cards nine times more often.

When the game imposes a three card limit - that's hardly fair to the
customer.

arcs) are 8-9 regular issues with a special additions if necessary.

it's more fun (because it's more interesting due to being
more difficult) to collect the rarer ones.

My argument has almost nothing to do with "collecting". To
me, it's all about *playing*. These cards belong to a game;
they're useful, IMO, primarily in that you use them to play
that game, and only secondarily in that they are an item
you can collect for fun and profit. Baseball cards are only
the second thing; poker cards are (more or less) only the
first thing; VTES cards are some of both, but it seems to me
that it serves the game a lot better if rarity decisions are
made based more on the gaming side of the equation than the
collecting side.

> Because everything shouldn't simply be served to you on a silver platter.
More
> people should do some work instead of whining incessently (not directed at
> anyone in particular).

I'm not talking about a silver platter here. I'm not saying
that every pack should have a Freak Drive in it. I'm just
saying that one Freak Drive per hundred packs isn't enough.
One per ten packs might be more reasonable.

It sounds to me - and I don't mean to be offensive - like
your POV focuses more on the fun of collecting the cards
than the playing fun, and that your idea of collecting fun
includes the coolness of having things that other people
don't have. Fair enough. But the fact that it's a game
as well as a collectible means that people need copies of
the high-utility card to be able to play competitively, and
it leads to an unbalanced tournament environment if they
can't get them relatively easily.

In "that other game" they don't really seem to care about
this, and it's taken for granted that you'll have to spend
$200+ on cards every three months if you want to compete
in tournaments. In VTES, I think most of the players would
consider than an exorbitant expenditure, and I think we'll
get more players interested in playing the game (*and*
buying and collecting cards) if they don't have to spend
*that* much to compete.

Josh

While Magic is likely the most expensive CCG to keep up with as new sets are
prolific, the most money intensive CCG per card, assuming you wanted to be
competitive at the top level, I played was Wheel of Time. Did that kill WoT?
No. Niche player base, screwing around with deciding what a new base set
should be like, and distributor apathy in a sluggish market killed the game.

CCGs are investments. I consider an initial minimum investment of $120 in a
CCG reasonable. To compete on a tournament level, looking at five times that
or so, minimum. As someone said, that's the equivalent of a number of
boardgames (or computer games or whatever). But, that's the market.

Realize that no one is forcing people to shell out this sort of money to play
CCGs, yet lots of people do.

Now, it is possible to spend less on CCGs and still have fun. As long as you
play with people with similar collection sizes, everything should be copacetic.
It's even possible to play some tournaments without dropping hundreds of
dollars - just find a CCG with a good limited, sealed deck or draft,
environment.

Anecdote: I got back into Magic late last year. I don't buy boxes like I used
to, though. I never see doing that again. I play a sealed league format. Low
cost and more fun.

Rock Cat also has an anti-weenie special.

Govern, or Enchant Kindred available. About the best way they can gain
pool is to use a Blood Doll/Minion Tap, and then superior Restoration to
refill the blood. This means it is going to be very difficult for a
Gargoyle deck to recruit multiple Rock Cats at 4 pool each.

combat, but that would be using a combat clan to do combat, and that's
not "cool" enough for Aaron.)

pool -- at the cost of a second action. The second action must be taken
by a Tremere or !Tremere ... probably a Tremere since there is only one
!Tremere slave Gargoyle. Of the Tremere, only 6 have Potence, and only

both 7-caps. This is sort of expensive -- however, you are perfectly
capable of using Roreca Quaid (who can at least play the sideline
discipline of all your VIS cards) if you want to.

Enter yet ANOTHER problem: Soul of the Earth is a +1 stealth action.
+1 intercept is extremely prevalent these days, largely because of such
actions as Soul of the Earth. Roreca Quaid can generate no additional
stealth on her actions. Competent players will block the Soul of the
Earth action if it is at all possible for them to do so, because it is
much better to get beaten up by one Gargoyle once than it is to get
beaten up by Rock Cat over and over.

There are only two Tremere with Obfuscate. One is an 8-cap, and one is
an 11-cap. Neither have Potence or Fortitude.

There are two Tremere with inherent +1 stealth on all actions. One has
Potence. One has Fortitude and free diablerie. Both of these are
definitely better choices than gluing OBF on Roreca Quaid or influencing
Justine, but now, again, you're paying 7-8 pool for the ability to
reduce your Rock Cats' cost by 3 each... until you've recruited 3 Rock
Cats, you were probably better off just paying the full Rock Cat cost.

For all practical purposes, it is going to be EXTREMELY difficult to
actually get more than 2-3 Rock Cats in play, not to mention the
difficulty inherent in keeping a 4-life non-regenerative combat ally
alive through multiple combats in which it's getting hit for 1, at
least. Therefore, Rock Cat is EMINENTLY well suited for a rare slot,

not really sure if it is/was a power-rares game, though I
do recall hearing from people who did play in tourneys that
it was.

lot to do with what CCGs become popular, but I do think it
may have more to do with which ones *stay* popular. VTES

arguments by suggesting that that's the only alternative. I think Josh was just
pointing to some problems in terms of highly useful, high-demand cards that are
probably way rarer than they should be in the context of the current game
environment - at least from a game player's perspective. While I realize that
(and I think Josh realizes that) there needs to be enough incentive for players
to buy enough product to give White Wolf enough demand to print more cards, I'd
like to think it's not necessary to create some of the existing situations on
purpose to make this game sell.

that it clearly could be an uncommon without anyone complaining that they're
pulling too many of these things out of their packs. I don't know why WotC
choose to make them rares. Maybe they were deliberately intended to be power
rares, in spite of their protests to the contrary. More likely, the WotC
designers didn't realize it was as useful as it was when they printed it.

correct the problem, the same way The Sabbat corrected the problem of players
desiring many more copies of Immortal Grapple. A discussion of whether that is,
in fact, true for Disarm and/or might be as true or more true for other cards
is in order.

all isn't very interesting. About all I find that goes on is people having
some kind of burr up their butt about making it too easy for the newbies to
get the good cards. (whirls finger). Whup, whup! Why should anyone care?
I guess if printing an uncommon Disarm is likely to drive White Wolf out of
business, then they shouldn't do it. But I don't think it's going to.

Fred

money producing the CCG than they would make doing something else (such

people seem to realize. It's not only if WW makes money - it's if they
make enough money to justify the TIME spent.

Actually, they mean almost precisely the same thing. Perhaps you understood
something different? The reason there are so many jokes about the Tremere
being unplayable is because they are very difficult to play. And even when
you play them very well with a well-made deck, they can fall against many
other well-played well-made decks. In general, the Tremere are a little bit
weak, like the Gangrel. Both clans can win, but not as easily as many other
clans. I really don't understand how every clan can be above-average, but
maybe some of you who think so will enlighten me...

Do you really want me to go into the reasons why Tremere are below-average?
It's all stuff you know, but I'll try and go through the motions, since you
appear to want me to...

The Tremere suffer mainly from a lack of offense. They have bleed, but they
have no stealth or unblockability. They have some titles, but no Princes
below 9 capacity, and they do not have Presence or any clan cards supporting
vote. So, aside from slightly odd decks, they are mostly relagated to
bleeding for their offense.

So... they have dominate for +bleed, but they have no stealth discipline.
So instead, we turn to bruise and bleed. Despite the rumours, Tremere are
not that great in combat. Theft of Vitae is a *great* first round strike,
but it's not going to torporize anyone, or save you if you get hit by a
combat deck. With no dodge w/add strike or damage prevention, the Tremere
have a hard time with combat defense in any case. Second round is when they
are supposed to shine. And Walk of Flame is definitely good. It's better
than Claws, but the thing is... since it requires 2 cards (the Walk and a
Press... which may be provided by a permanent in play, but those have their
own limitations) and a second round of combat, it's not really *enough*
better than Claws to build a really destructive deck around it. Telepathic
Tracking helps a lot, now that they finally have it, but you have to pack as
many TT's as your opponent has S:CE. You can use Thoughts Betrayed for
defense *and* offense, but it's quite expensive. You can Theft it back, but
if you're already low on blood, you have problems. The other 2nd round
combat cards are worse than Walk by varying degrees. Thaumaturgy combat is,
simply put, not as effective as Potence combat.

On the flip side, you have intercept combat decks. These could possibly
win, but with the new Game Wins rule, it's a losing strategy. You pretty
much need to have voting power to pass through your Dramtic Upheaval and get
you into the sweet spot, in order to have a chance at a table win. Like I
said, the Tremere are a little low on voting power.

What it all boils down to is a clan that is low on (pool-destruction)
offense and weak in combat defense. It is very good at pool-destruction
defense, but only so-so at combat offense.

Gangrel, on the other hand, have almost the opposite problem. They have
stealth but no bleed discipline, and have tons of combat power, but no real
way to affect pool loss (offensively or defensively), other than semi-decent
intercept.

This is not to say that trick decks cannot be made with either clan that
work great, but the clans as a whole are a little weak, due mainly to
discipline mix. And those trick decks really aren't unbeatable either.

gave one argument in favor of the Gargoyles, which I will restate:
